lesson_title: Lift a Boulder With One Hand
hook_text: 800 newtons of rock. One person. A bar and a stone. How is that possible?
clip_script: A boulder sits in a field near Polokwane. It weighs about 800 newtons, far more than anyone can lift. The worker slides a steel bar under it, wedges a stone under the bar close to the rock, and pushes down on the far end. The boulder rises. Three words explain it. The stone is the pivot. The boulder is the load. The push is the effort. Because the push is far from the pivot and the rock is close to it, the bar multiplies the force. Load divided by effort: 800 over 100 is a mechanical advantage of 8. Eight times stronger. But look at the hands. They move 40 centimetres and the rock rises 5. Less force, more distance. That is the deal every lever makes, and the same deal your rescue device will make when a tiny syringe push becomes a grip strong enough to hold.
visual_style: Whiteboard side view of a bar on a stone under a boulder; arrows for effort and load, the pivot slides and the arrows change size.
mood: Curious and satisfying, the trick revealed by three labels.
pacing: Quick impossible setup, slow labelling of three words, snappy number, closing trade-off.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and find the pivot, load and effort on three tools at home.
